name: LL-37
subclass: Human cathelicidin; C-terminal effector peptide of hCAP18
status_note: LL-37 is a natural human peptide, not a licensed medicine; the synthetic version (INN ropocamptide) reached phase 2b for venous leg ulcers but has no marketing authorisation anywhere.
evidence_note: Its biology in humans is very well established, but as a drug it has only reached small phase 1–2 studies: a 2014 randomised phase 2a in leg ulcers was positive on healing predictors, while the larger 2021 phase 2b missed its primary endpoint.
tagline: The only human cathelicidin: an antimicrobial peptide that also steers immunity
summary: LL-37 is the single cathelicidin peptide made by humans, released from the hCAP18 precursor in neutrophils, skin and mucosal surfaces. It punches holes in bacterial membranes, but it is at least as important as a signal: it recruits immune cells, promotes wound repair and, when it binds self-DNA, drives the interferon response that underlies psoriasis. Vitamin D switches on the gene that makes it. A synthetic version, ropocamptide, has been tested topically on chronic leg ulcers.
overview: Cathelicidins are host-defence peptides kept as inactive precursors with a conserved 'cathelin' pro-domain. Cattle and pigs have several; humans and mice have just one gene each (mouse Camp encodes the related peptide CRAMP). The human gene, CAMP, encodes hCAP18, which is stored in neutrophil specific granules and made by keratinocytes and epithelial cells throughout the airways, gut and urogenital tract. Proteinase 3 released from the same neutrophils cleaves hCAP18 outside the cell to free the 37-residue C-terminal peptide, which begins with two leucines — hence LL-37.

The peptide was described independently in the mid-1990s. Agerberth and colleagues in Stockholm predicted it from a bone-marrow cDNA and called the 39-residue form FALL-39, while groups in Copenhagen and California characterised the hCAP18 precursor and its neutrophil storage; the physiological 37-residue product and its proteinase 3 processing were pinned down by Sørensen and Borregaard in 2001. In water LL-37 is largely unstructured but oligomeric; on contact with anionic membranes or detergent micelles it folds into an amphipathic α-helix, and crystal structures show it forming dimers, fibril-like assemblies and even a tetrameric channel.

Its direct antibacterial action — membrane permeabilisation of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, plus activity against some fungi and enveloped viruses — is only part of the story. LL-37 is chemotactic through FPR2, transactivates the EGF receptor in keratinocytes, promotes angiogenesis and re-epithelialisation, and neutralises LPS. A landmark 2006 Science paper showed that Toll-like receptor engagement on macrophages induces the vitamin D receptor and the enzyme that makes active vitamin D, which then switches on CAMP — a mechanism that finally gave a molecular basis to the old observation that vitamin D deficiency predisposes to tuberculosis.

The same properties make LL-37 harmful when it is made in the wrong place. In psoriasis it complexes with self-DNA and RNA released from damaged skin and converts them into potent activators of plasmacytoid dendritic cells through TLR9 and TLR7, driving type I interferon; LL-37 is also a T-cell autoantigen in a large fraction of patients. In rosacea, abnormal processing by kallikrein 5 generates fragments that provoke inflammation and vascular change. As a therapeutic, synthetic LL-37 under the non-proprietary name ropocamptide has been taken through topical wound-healing trials by the Swedish company Promore Pharma; a separate line of work has injected it into melanoma lesions. Grey-market vendors also sell LL-37 vials for self-administration, a use with no supporting clinical evidence and a plausible autoimmune hazard.
mechanism: LL-37 carries a net charge of about +6 at physiological pH and, once folded, separates into a hydrophobic face and a cationic face. It is drawn electrostatically to the anionic surfaces of bacterial membranes and lipopolysaccharide, then inserts and disrupts them, most probably by a carpet-like or toroidal-pore mechanism rather than a single discrete channel; cholesterol-rich mammalian membranes are much less susceptible, which is what gives the peptide its selectivity.

Its immune effects run through receptors. LL-37 is a chemoattractant for neutrophils, monocytes and T cells via the formyl peptide receptor FPR2/FPRL1, transactivates EGFR in keratinocytes to drive migration and wound closure, and binds and neutralises LPS to limit endotoxin-driven inflammation. It also modulates inflammasome and purinergic signalling in monocytes.

The pathological arm is nucleic-acid chaperoning. Cationic LL-37 condenses extracellular self-DNA and self-RNA into aggregated complexes that resist degradation and are delivered into the endosomes of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, where they trigger TLR9 and TLR7 and a strong type I interferon response. This breaks tolerance to self nucleic acids and is a core mechanism in psoriasis, with parallels in lupus.
origin: Natural human peptide: the C-terminal 37 residues (positions 134–170) of the cathelicidin precursor hCAP18, encoded by the CAMP gene

discovery.by: Birgitta Agerberth, Gudmundur Gudmundsson and colleagues, with parallel work by Niels Borregaard's and Robert Lehrer's groups
discovery.where: Karolinska Institute, Stockholm; Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen; UCLA
discovery.note: Agerberth's 1995 PNAS paper predicted a cysteine-free human peptide antibiotic from a bone-marrow cDNA and named the 39-residue form FALL-39; the 37-residue LL-37 released from hCAP18 by proteinase 3 was defined by Sørensen and colleagues in 2001.

developer: Promore Pharma AB (Solna, Sweden) develops synthetic LL-37 under the non-proprietary name ropocamptide

analogs.name: KR-12
analogs.note: The smallest fragment of LL-37 that retains antibacterial activity (residues 18–29); used as a template for shorter, less cytotoxic derivatives.

analogs.name: GF-17 / LL-37(17–29)
analogs.note: Core helical fragments that keep most of the antimicrobial potency with reduced haemolysis; several have been crystallised.

analogs.name: ALL-38
analogs.note: A 38-residue variant generated in seminal plasma when gastricsin cleaves hCAP18 at the acidic pH of the vagina.

analogs.name: CAP-18 (rabbit)
analogs.note: The rabbit cathelicidin after which the human precursor hCAP18 was named.

targets.name: Formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2/FPRL1)
targets.action: Agonist — chemotaxis of neutrophils, monocytes and T cells

targets.name: Toll-like receptor 9
targets.action: Indirect activation — LL-37–self-DNA complexes trigger TLR9 in plasmacytoid dendritic cells

targets.name: Epidermal growth factor receptor
targets.action: Transactivation in keratinocytes, driving migration and re-epithelialisation

targets.name: P2X7 receptor
targets.action: Modulation of inflammasome and IL-1β release in monocytes

targets.name: Bacterial membranes and lipopolysaccharide
targets.action: Electrostatic binding and permeabilisation; LPS neutralisation

sequence.note: All 37 residues are standard L-amino acids and the peptide contains no cysteine, so there are no disulfide bridges — unusual among host-defence peptides. The numbering offset of 133 maps position 1 onto residue 134 of the hCAP18 precursor (UniProt P49913); the literature normally numbers the peptide 1–37 in its own right. The 39-residue form originally reported as FALL-39 begins two residues earlier.

half_life: Not established; the synthetic peptide is used topically rather than systemically

structure.notes: LL-37 is disordered in dilute aqueous buffer and only folds on contact with anionic membranes or detergents, so every experimental structure captures a membrane-associated or crystal-packed state. Structures of shorter fragments (KR-12, GF-17, LL-23) and of LL-37 captured by a streptococcal M protein are also available.

investigational.detail: A 2014 phase 2a in 34 patients found six- and threefold higher healing-rate constants at the two lower doses; the 148-patient HEAL LL-37 phase 2b found no overall difference from placebo, with a post-hoc signal in ulcers larger than 10 cm².
A topical LL-37 cream was registered for study in Indonesia against bacterial colonisation, inflammation and healing rate.
A single-centre study of intratumoral LL-37 injection at MD Anderson enrolled only four participants.

investigational.use: Raising endogenous LL-37 rather than giving it
investigational.detail: Vitamin D, sodium butyrate and phenylbutyrate have all been trialled as inducers of the CAMP gene in tuberculosis, diarrhoeal disease and critical illness, with mixed results.

off_label.detail: Sold online as a research peptide for chronic infection, Lyme disease, gut and skin complaints, usually for subcutaneous self-injection.
off_label.evidence: No clinical trial supports systemic use. Given LL-37's established role in driving interferon responses to self-DNA in psoriasis and lupus, administering it outside a trial carries a specific theoretical autoimmune risk, on top of the usual sterility and purity concerns.

off_label.detail: Marketed in some skin preparations on the basis of its wound-healing and antimicrobial biology.
off_label.evidence: The only controlled human data are the two venous-leg-ulcer trials, and the larger of those was negative overall.

history.title: A human cathelicidin is predicted from cDNA
history.detail: Agerberth and colleagues reported FALL-39, a cysteine-free putative human peptide antibiotic expressed in bone marrow and testis.

history.title: hCAP18 located in neutrophil granules
history.detail: Sørensen, Cowland and Borregaard showed the precursor is made in myelocytes and metamyelocytes and stored in specific granules, and developed an ELISA for it in plasma.

history.title: Proteinase 3 releases the active peptide
history.detail: Sørensen and colleagues identified extracellular cleavage of hCAP18 by proteinase 3 as the step that generates LL-37 itself.

history.title: A second processing route in seminal plasma
history.detail: Gastricsin was shown to cleave hCAP18 to the 38-residue ALL-38 at vaginal pH, a distinct mechanism for generating an antimicrobial peptide after intercourse.

history.title: Vitamin D switches the gene on
history.detail: Liu, Modlin and colleagues showed in Science that Toll-like receptor signalling induces the vitamin D receptor and CYP27B1 in macrophages, leading to cathelicidin expression and killing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

history.title: Rosacea linked to abnormal cathelicidin processing
history.detail: Yamasaki and Gallo reported that increased kallikrein-5 activity in rosacea generates cathelicidin fragments that drive skin inflammation and vascular change.

history.title: LL-37 turns self-DNA into an interferon trigger
history.detail: Lande and colleagues showed in Nature that LL-37–DNA complexes activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells through TLR9, explaining a core step in psoriasis.

history.title: First NMR structure of the whole peptide
history.detail: Guangshun Wang solved LL-37 and its minimal fragment KR-12 in lipid micelles, defining the amphipathic helix and the smallest active core.

history.title: Positive first-in-man trial in venous leg ulcers
history.detail: In 34 patients, twice-weekly topical LL-37 at 0.5 and 1.6 mg/mL gave roughly six- and threefold higher healing-rate constants than placebo, with no safety signal; the highest dose did not work.

history.title: Crystallography reveals oligomers
history.detail: A series of structures showed LL-37 crystallising as monomers, dimers and fibril-like assemblies depending on the detergent present, suggesting oligomers are the membrane-active species.

history.title: HEAL LL-37 phase 2b misses its endpoint
history.detail: In 148 patients with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers, topical ropocamptide plus compression did not improve healing overall; a post-hoc analysis suggested benefit confined to ulcers of at least 10 cm².

history.title: A pathogen is caught hiding from it
history.detail: Structures of a streptococcal M protein capturing LL-37, and of a gonococcal efflux pump binding it, showed how bacteria actively evade the peptide.

history.title: Still no approved product
history.detail: Ropocamptide remains in development for chronic wounds with no marketing authorisation in any region, while LL-37 continues to be sold through unregulated peptide vendors.

regulatory.detail: No FDA-approved LL-37 product; investigational use only. Material sold online is labelled for research use.
Ropocamptide has been studied in EU clinical trials (Sweden, Poland) but holds no marketing authorisation.

Not named on the Prohibited List, but category S0 covers any pharmacological substance with no current approval by a governmental regulatory health authority for human therapeutic use, which applies to LL-37 preparations.

pk.bioavailability: Studied topically; systemic absorption from wound dressings was not a measurable feature of the leg-ulcer trials
pk.metabolism: Degraded by host and bacterial proteases; plasma concentrations of the hCAP18 precursor are the usual clinical biomarker rather than free LL-37

dosing_note: There is no approved human dose. In the venous-leg-ulcer trials the peptide was applied topically at 0.5, 1.6 or 3.2 mg/mL twice weekly under compression; notably the highest concentration performed no better than placebo, which is a reason not to treat 'more' as 'better'. No systemic regimen has been established in any trial.

common: Local application-site reactions in topical trials
serious: Haemolysis and cytotoxicity at high concentrations in vitro
Theoretical risk of provoking interferon-driven autoimmunity, given the peptide's established role in psoriasis and lupus
warnings: Topical LL-37 was well tolerated at 0.5–3.2 mg/mL in trials, but no systemic route has been formally assessed for safety in humans
Elevated cathelicidin is part of the disease process in psoriasis and rosacea, so administering it to people with these conditions is a specific concern
Peptide sold through unregulated vendors has unverified identity, purity, endotoxin content and sterility
safety.notes: Selectivity for bacterial over human membranes is only relative: the peptide is cytotoxic to mammalian cells above roughly the concentrations needed for antibacterial action, which has been a recurring obstacle to developing it as a systemic antibiotic.

facts: Humans and mice each have a single cathelicidin gene, but the mouse peptide CRAMP differs from LL-37 in sequence and activity, which complicates extrapolating mouse infection studies to people.
LL-37 is named for its first two residues (Leu-Leu) and its length (37), the same naming convention that produced FALL-39, LL-23 and KR-12.
It contains no cysteine at all, unlike the disulfide-locked defensins it works alongside.
The vitamin D response element in the CAMP gene promoter arrived in primates via a transposable element, which is why the vitamin D–cathelicidin link exists in humans but not in mice.
Sunlight-driven vitamin D synthesis raising cathelicidin is the molecular echo of the pre-antibiotic 'heliotherapy' once used for tuberculosis.
